clinical_record:
A 55-year-old white woman with a history of diverticulosis and colonic polyps presented with new-onset flulike symptoms followed by low-grade fever, facial crusted plaques, and 4 weeks of bloody and watery diarrhea. Her facial lesions initially presented as ill-defined pink patches over her cheeks and red papules on her forehead. Over the next 4 days, the lesions spread to her chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock, and a single papule appeared on the right lower extremity. Her low-grade fevers and diarrhea persisted throughout this 4-day period.

In the emergency department, she was febrile and tachycardic. Physical findings included:- 6 × 7-cm well-demarcated vegetative crusted plaques on the bilateral cheeks- Several discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaques on the temple- Discrete pustules, vesicles, and umbilicated papules on cheeks and temple- Lesions on chest, abdomen, back, and left buttock- Painful subcutaneous nodules over lower extremities- Polyarthralgia

Laboratory Tests:- Mild leukocytosis with normal differential- Mildly elevated transaminase and alkaline phosphatase levels- Negative wound culture- Blood cultures showed no growth- Negative PCR for herpes simplex virus- Negative direct fluorescent antibody assay for varicella-zoster virusPathology:- Forehead lesion biopsy: Intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration and intracorneal neutrophils. Special stains negative for microorganisms- Right thigh biopsy: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas- Colonoscopy: Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colonImages:Image 1 Title: Clinical Appearance of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 1 Description: A, A 6 × 7-cm, well-demarcated, vegetative crusted plaque on the left cheek and a discrete, round, 1- to 2-cm crusted plaque on the foreheadImage 2 Title: Histopathological Findings of Facial Neutrophilic DermatosisImage 2 Description: Shave biopsy specimen from forehead lesion showing diffuse intradermal neutrophilic infiltrate with central ulceration

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: IBD-associated neutrophilic dermatosis with ulcerative colitis

decisive_spans: IBD-associated neutrophilic dermatosis
ulcerative colitis
Colonoscopy: Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colon
reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes a patient with symptoms and findings consistent with neutrophilic dermatosis (facial crusted plaques, pustules, vesicles, umbilicated papules, intradermal neutrophilic inflammation) and inflammatory bowel disease (4 weeks of bloody and watery diarrhea, colonoscopy showing moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colon). The colonoscopy findings are characteristic of ulcerative colitis.

decisive_spans: Septal panniculitis with Miescher radial granulomas
Intradermal neutrophilic inflammation with ulceration
Moderate inflammation, edema, erosions, and pseudopolyps in the sigmoid colon
reviewer_b.rationale: The record shows neutrophilic dermatosis with Sweet syndrome features (Miescher radial granulomas, dermal neutrophilia) and colonic inflammation with pseudopolyps, but does not explicitly state inflammatory bowel disease or ulcerative colitis. The colonoscopy findings suggest IBD but are not diagnostic of ulcerative colitis specifically, and no direct assertion of IBD is present.

clinical_record:

The patient had a 3-year history of hypertension but no history of neurological disorders. The patient was alert and oriented.

- Effacement of the right frontal wrinkle- Incomplete closure of the right eyelid- Flattening of the right nasolabial fold- Muscle strength in the right upper and lower extremities: grade 0/5- Hypoesthesia noted on the right side- Right Babinski sign: positive

- Imaging Studies:  1. Emergency CT scan of the head:     Image Title: Cranial computed tomography     Image Description: Hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region and in the lateral ventricle at 24 hours postonset    2. Cerebral MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging (1 week and 1 month after onset):     Image Description: No definitive lesions in the brainstem or evidence of hemorrhage-related iron deposition in the ventral part of the pons    3. Cerebral MRI with diffusion tensor imaging (1 month after onset):     Image Description: Corticobulbar tract appeared thinner on the left side than on the right before entering the brainstem

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Ipsilateral hemisphere hemorrhagic stroke with peripheral-type facial paralysis

decisive_spans: Hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region
incomplete closure of the right eye
flattening of the right nasolabial fold
reviewer_a.rationale: The record clearly indicates a hemorrhagic stroke involving the thalamus and radiation crown, along with facial paralysis. However, it does not explicitly state 'ipsilateral hemisphere' or 'peripheral-type facial paralysis'. The facial paralysis is described as incomplete closure of the right eye and flattening of the right nasolabial fold, which are signs of facial nerve involvement, but the specific 'peripheral-type' is not explicitly stated. The hemiplegia is contralateral to the hemorrhage, making 'ipsilateral hemisphere' for the stroke component unclear or potentially conflicting if referring to the side of the hemorrhage.

decisive_spans: Hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region and in the lateral ventricle at 24 hours postonset
Corticobulbar tract appeared thinner on the left side than on the right before entering the brainstem
Incomplete closure of the right eyelid
reviewer_b.rationale: The record explicitly describes left-hemisphere hemorrhage and right-sided hemiplegia with facial paralysis features (incomplete eyelid closure, flattened nasolabial fold) consistent with peripheral-type facial paralysis. clinical_record:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a large unhealed ulcer measuring 20 × 14-cm² that had persisted for the past 3 years. The patient had a patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on her left forearm. Blood cell genotyping revealed compound heterozygous alterations (c.2992 + 2T>G and c.8621-30A>G) at splice sites in COL7A1.

The patient presented with:- A 20 × 14-cm² persistent ulcer on the back- A patch of healthy skin (7.5 × 4 cm²) on the left forearm, lacking blistering

1. Genetic Testing:- Blood cell genotyping showed compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1- RNA transcript analysis using MinION platform:  * Affected skin epidermis: Dominant RNA transcripts with premature stop codons, wild-type reads rare (1.1%)  * Potentially revertant area epidermis: High rates of wild-type transcripts (35.0%)  * Revertant skin dermis: Wild-type reads rare (1.9%)2. Microscopy:- Immunofluorescence and transmission electron microscopy of the grafted area showed type VII collagen and anchoring fibrilsImages:- Figure 1A: Sanger sequencing showing compound heterozygous COL7A1 alteration- Figure 1B: Image of the persistent ulcer on patient's back- Figure 1C: Image of revertant skin patch on left forearm

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Severe generalized recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB) with revertant mosaicism

A 20 × 14-cm² persistent ulcer on the back
Potentially revertant area epidermis: High rates of wild-type transcripts (35.0%)
reviewer_a.rationale: The presence of compound heterozygous alterations in COL7A1, a large persistent ulcer, and evidence of revertant mosaicism (high rates of wild-type transcripts in a potentially revertant area) strongly support the full reference diagnosis of severe generalized recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa with revertant mosaicism.

decisive_spans: compound heterozygous alterations (c.2992 + 2T>G and c.8621-30A>G) at splice sites in COL7A1
High rates of wild-type transcripts (35.0%)
type VII collagen and anchoring fibrils

clinical_record:
A patient in their 60s presented to the emergency department with approximately 20 minutes of acute, severe precordial chest pain radiating to their left arm at night, accompanied by dyspnea, dizziness, and sweating. The patient's medical history was notable for hypertension, cerebral infarction, diabetes, and nicotine addiction.

Vital signs showed blood pressure of 188/101 mm Hg, heart rate at 84 beats/min, and respiratory rate at 20 breaths/min.

- Laboratory tests:
  - Serum cardiac troponin I level: <0.05 ng/mL (normal range, <0.16 ng/mL)
  - Potassium level: 4.1 mEq/L (normal range, 3.5-5.3 mEq/L)

- ECG findings:
  Image A Title: Initial ECG
  Image A Description: ECG showed a sinus rhythm at a rate of 85 beats/min with the presence of broad-based, asymmetrical, tall upright T waves in precordial leads V2 through V5

  Image B Title: Post-procedural ECG
  Image B Description: Sinus rhythm at 65 beats/min with normalization of the T-wave morphology in leads V2 through V5

- Coronary angiography:
  Finding: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes an acute myocardial infarction based on symptoms, ECG findings (tall T waves in V2-V5, later normalizing), and coronary angiography (subtotal occlusion of LAD). However, the troponin I level is normal, which typically argues against an MI. The reference diagnosis includes 'Window-Period', which implies a specific timing relative to biomarker elevation that is not explicitly supported or refuted by the provided information. The normal troponin makes 'Window-Period' a plausible explanation for the lack of biomarker elevation in the presence of other strong MI indicators, but the record does not provide enough information to definitively confirm this specific temporal aspect.

decisive_spans: Subtotal occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery
broad-based, asymmetrical, tall upright T waves in precordial leads V2 through V5
Serum cardiac troponin I level: <0.05 ng/mL
reviewer_b.rationale: The record supports acute myocardial infarction due to acute coronary occlusion with ischemic ECG changes, but the normal troponin and lack of ST elevation or other timing details do not uniquely establish the 'window-period' (early phase before biomarker elevation) specificity. The reference is a plausible inference but not uniquely supported.
unsupported_components: acute myocardial infarction subtype (STEMI vs NSTEMI)

clinical_record:
A woman in her 30s with a history of right breast cancer, stage IIIa (cT2N2M0). She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by right modified radical mastectomy and postoperative radiotherapy. After radiotherapy, she noticed a pruritic erythema lesion with multiple nodules over the operation site of the right breast. The lesion did not respond to initial topical treatments. Three months later (1 year after initial cancer diagnosis), she presented to dermatology for evaluation of skin erythema over her right breast.

A well-demarcated, warm, erythematous plaque, 15 × 12 cm, was seen over the right side of the anterior chest wall around her operation scar. Scattered within the erythema were multiple palpable small nodules.

- Immunohistochemistry:   Negative for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)- Skin Biopsy:  Multiple emboli of carcinoma cells in dermal and subcutaneous lymphatic vessels- Images:  Image Title: Postmastectomy Clinical Images Before and After Treatment  Image Description A: Right mastectomy scar with a large well-defined area of erythema and multiple, scattered small nodules  Image Description B: Nearly complete remission of skin lesions after treatment

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Carcinoma erysipelatoides arising from triple-negative breast cancer

pruritic erythema lesion with multiple nodules over the operation site of the right breast

The prior history of right breast cancer, specifically negative for ER, PR, and HER2, confirms the triple-negative breast cancer origin.

pruritic erythema lesion with multiple nodules over the operation site of the right breast

clinical_record:
A man in his 60s presented with a lesion on the left lower eyelid. His ocular history was notable for a traumatic icicle injury as a child that resulted in loss of the left eye. He had surgery to place an implant into the eye socket, and approximately 14 years prior underwent a lower eyelid reconstruction. He had excellent prosthesis position without need for refitting or replacement for more than 10 years until recently noting that his ocular prosthesis would spontaneously extrude from his anophthalmic socket.

On examination, he had a small, pearly lesion in the tear trough region of the left lower eyelid that had been growing over the past few months. He had contraction of the conjunctival mucosal tissue across the fornix of the left lower eyelid and increased scleral show of his ocular prosthesis with shortening of his lower eyelid skin. His prosthesis was extruded from his socket due to cicatricial effects causing conjunctival shrinkage and eyelid skin contracture.

- Imaging:  Image Title: Local Recurrence Within Electronic Surface Brachytherapy Field  Image Description: An elevated, pearly lesion on the left lower eyelid with scleral show on the prosthetic eye of the left lateral lower eyelid, showing conjunctival forniceal shortening with extrusion of the prosthesis and cicatricial shortening of the lower eyelid skin- Pathology:  Initial shave biopsy revealed nodular BCC of the left cheek  Subsequent biopsy specimen showed infiltrative pattern with no signs of fibrosis or inflammatory infiltrate

recurrent

clinical_record:
A man in his 30s presented with a mass in the right nostril that had been growing for about 1 year. The lesion bled with minimal trauma but did not obstruct his breathing. The patient did not smoke and denied any medical history of chronic rhinosinusitis.

Physical examination revealed a 1-cm, nontender, exophytic, verrucous, skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule.

- Histologic examination:  Image Title: Histologic sections (Figure C)  Image Description: Papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores that are lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium (original magnification ×200)    Image Title: Higher magnification histology (Figure D)  Image Description: Shows mucin-containing goblet cells. Neither cytologic atypia nor atypical mitotic figures are present (original magnification ×400)    Clinical Images:  Image Title: Clinical presentation (Figure A and B)  Image Description: An exophytic, verrucous, and skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Shows mucin-containing goblet cells. Neither cytologic atypia nor atypical mitotic figures are present
reviewer_a.rationale: The histological findings are consistent with Schneiderian papilloma, characterized by papillary fronds lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium and goblet cells without atypia. However, the specific 'exophytic' subtype is not explicitly confirmed by the histology, which describes papillary fronds, a feature common to all Schneiderian papillomas. The clinical description of an 'exophytic plaque' describes the gross appearance, but 'exophytic' as a specific histological subtype (e.g., fungiform) is not definitively stated or implied by the microscopic description alone.

CT scan with contrast of thorax and brain showed lesions in the liver and brain

clinical_record:
A healthy male toddler presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain and distention, fever, and vomiting of 1 day's duration. He was found to have 'bruises' on both flanks. Over the next 2 days, he developed diffuse papules on the trunk and extremities; his condition rapidly deteriorated requiring intubation, vasopressors, and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Purpuric retiform patches were found on each flank (1 of them studded with 2 pustules) with erythematous to violaceous papules diffusely scattered on the extremities and trunk.

- Laboratory tests:  - Hyponatremia and neutropenia present  - AST: 45 U/L  - ALT: 142 U/L   - C-reactive protein: >270 mg/L  - Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 43 mm/h  - Ferritin: 603 ng/mL  - Urinalysis showed proteinuria and hematuria- Imaging studies:  - CT chest/abdomen: Cavitary lesions in lungs representing necrotizing pneumonia. Areas of nonenhancement within both kidneys suspected to represent renal abscesses  - MRI brain: Multifocal lesions, likely septic emboli  - Transthoracic echocardiogram: Negative  - Bone scans: Negative- Pathological tests:  - Punch biopsy findings:    - Frozen section: Small organisms within vasculature    - Permanent sections: Large neutrophilic pustule with inflammation throughout dermis and prominent necrosis with basophilic structures filling necrotic vascular spaces    - Tissue Gram staining: Gram-positive cocci in vessels  - Tissue culture, blood culture, bronchial washings, and fluid from bilateral empyemas all showed positive results

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) sepsis with septic vasculopathy

decisive_spans: Tissue Gram staining: Gram-positive cocci in vessels
Tissue culture, blood culture, bronchial washings, and fluid from bilateral empyemas all showed positive results
Purpuric retiform patches were found on each flank
reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record provides strong evidence for all components of the reference diagnosis. Sepsis is indicated by the rapid deterioration, intubation, vasopressors, and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP >270 mg/L, ESR 43 mm/h). The causative organism, Staphylococcus aureus, is identified by Gram stain (Gram-positive cocci) and multiple positive cultures (tissue, blood, bronchial washings, empyema fluid). The 'community-acquired' aspect is supported by the patient being a healthy toddler presenting from home. Methicillin-resistance is not explicitly stated but is a common and often assumed characteristic in severe S. aureus infections without specific susceptibility testing mentioned. Septic vasculopathy is evidenced by the 'purpuric retiform patches' and 'bruises' on flanks, 'prominent necrosis with basophilic structures filling necrotic vascular spaces' on biopsy, and 'small organisms within vasculature'.

decisive_spans: Gram-positive cocci in vessels
Tissue culture, blood culture, bronchial washings, and fluid from bilateral empyemas all showed positive results
Purpuric retiform patches
reviewer_b.rationale: The record confirms staphylococcal sepsis with septic emboli and vasculitis-like skin lesions, but does not specify methicillin resistance or acquisition setting. 'Septic vasculopathy' is a descriptive term not explicitly stated; the findings support a septic vasculopathic process but the exact term is not uniquely identified.

clinical_record:
A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. What is the most likely diagnosis?

The record mentions "dilated, tortuous veins" but does not definitively characterize them as a venous malformation in the context of the syndrome.

hypertrophy of the left thigh, overgrowth of both feet

She denied any history of psoriasis. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, hypoproteinemia, transaminitis, and an elevated C‐reactive protein level. Skin biopsies from the back demonstrated separation of the stratum corneum with multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils, underlying spongiotic epidermis with neutrophilic exocytosis, papillary dermal edema, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

widespread erythema, desquamation, and pustulation
multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils

A 52-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV (viral load <40 copies/mL, CD4 count 290 cells/mm3) was found to have a 20% weight loss (12 kg) over one year, initially intentional but accelerating in recent months. She reported no fevers, night sweats, gastrointestinal symptoms, or gynecological complaints. On examination, there was a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Laboratory studies showed a drop in hemoglobin from 13 g/dL to 10 g/dL, a lactate dehydrogenase level of 643 U/L, a C-reactive protein level of 80 mg/L, and a normal white-cell count. Her past history included a hysterectomy for micro-invasive cervical carcinoma in 2002; no operative records were available. An urgent CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 15 cm mass possibly arising from the vaginal wall with a potential fistulous connection to the cecum, and mesenteric lymph nodes measuring up to 27 mm but no distant metastases. Serum tumor markers (CA19-9, CEA, CA125) were all negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes a patient with a mass, weight loss, elevated LDH and CRP, and lymphadenopathy, which are all consistent with lymphoma. However, there is no specific information (e.g., biopsy results, immunohistochemistry) to identify the specific subtype as 'diffuse large B-cell lymphoma'. The record only suggests a mass and lymph nodes, which could be various types of lymphoma or other malignancies.

decisive_spans: 20% weight loss (12 kg) over one year
lactate dehydrogenase level of 643 U/L
15 cm mass possibly arising from the vaginal wall
reviewer_b.rationale: The case supports a lymphoma family (B symptoms, elevated LDH, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, pelvic mass) but provides no histologic, immunophenotypic, or cytogenetic evidence to specifically identify the diffuse large B-cell lymphoma subtype.

clinical_record:
A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

On examination he was afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. General and neurologic exams were unremarkable. He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC, renal function, and albumin; γ‐glutamyl transferase was elevated at 81 IU/L (normal < 55) and total bilirubin 26 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5). Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: COVID-19-associated acute and transient psychotic disorder

decisive_spans: COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive
escalating behavioral changes
talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions
reviewer_a.rationale: The patient presented with acute psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, insomnia) and tested positive for COVID-19. The symptoms are described as acute and transient, fitting the 'acute and transient psychotic disorder' component.

decisive_spans: A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.
episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions
He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated
reviewer_b.rationale: The record clearly supports COVID-19 infection and an acute psychotic presentation, but does not explicitly document the specific diagnostic subtype 'acute and transient psychotic disorder' or rule out other psychotic disorders; the reference's full specificity is not uniquely supported by the record.
unsupported_components: acute and transient psychotic disorder (specific subtype not explicitly stated in record)

clinical_record:
A 52-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology in 2011 for a 2-month history of right-sided neck swelling, worsening dysphagia, and mild pain. Her past medical history was notable for excision of a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in the left inguinal–suprapubic region in 1998, with four local recurrences (2000, 2001, 2008, and 2009) treated surgically; she also received external radiotherapy (66 Gy) after the last excision.

On examination, there was a large, firm, mildly tender mass on the right side of the neck without fixation; the Pemberton sign was positive. Laboratory studies showed:
• TSH 0.363 mIU/L (0.32–5.0)  
• Free T4 14.6 pmol/L (9.0–19.0)  
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody 1 U/mL (< 1)  
• Intact PTH 6 pmol/L (1.48–8.43)

Ultrasound of the thyroid revealed a right lobe volume of 50 mL and left lobe 7.3 mL; the entire right lobe was replaced by a hypo- to anechoic mass measuring approximately 6 × 4 × 6 cm, displacing the trachea 1 cm to the left, with no pathological lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the right lobe yielded a hemorrhagic background with isolated clusters of pleomorphic round and oval nuclei; it was classified as category IV/3, suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and thorax confirmed a voluminous right thyroid mass and detected two pulmonary nodules consistent with metastases. MRI showed no lymphadenopathy. Laryngoscopy demonstrated freely mobile vocal cords.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes a patient with a history of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and a new thyroid mass with pulmonary nodules. While the history of DFSP is clear, the reference diagnosis 'dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans' alone does not specify the metastatic nature or the site of metastasis (thyroid) which is implied by the case presentation. The FNA was suspicious for primary or secondary malignancy, but did not definitively confirm DFSP metastasis to the thyroid.

decisive_spans: dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
four local recurrences
external radiotherapy (66 Gy)
reviewer_b.rationale: The record explicitly documents a history of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) with multiple local recurrences and radiotherapy, and the current presentation is a thyroid mass with pulmonary nodules. The reference diagnosis is DFSP metastasizing to the thyroid, which is supported by the history and metastatic pattern, though no biopsy of the thyroid confirming DFSP is mentioned.

A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

decisive_spans: 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus
Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant
reviewer_a.rationale: The CT findings describe a multiloculated mass extending from the bladder dome to the umbilicus, which is characteristic of a urachal cyst. The differential diagnoses listed by the author also include urachal cyst (implied by 'urachal diverticulum' and 'patent urachus' which are related urachal anomalies, and the mass description fits a cyst).

decisive_spans: differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant
4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus
reviewer_b.rationale: The record describes a urachal remnant anomaly with imaging features and a differential list that includes several specific urachal entities, but does not uniquely identify a urachal cyst over other urachal anomalies or malignancy. The reference diagnosis is a specific subtype within the urachal remnant family, and the record does not provide enough detail to distinguish it from the other listed possibilities.
unsupported_components: specific urachal anomaly type (cyst vs sinus vs diverticulum vs patent urachus)

A 74-year-old man with a history of interstitial pneumonia presented with one month of right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area, accompanied by a cold sensation. He denied abnormal sensation or muscle weakness. Six months earlier, chest CT had shown dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes; on admission these shadows had enlarged. Oral antibiotic therapy failed to improve the infiltrates, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, he was sweating profusely on the right arm and right thorax. Vital signs were blood pressure 150/78 mmHg, pulse 71/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. A pleural friction rub was heard over the right chest. The skin on the right arm, chest, and back was moister and cooler than the left. Thermography revealed decreased surface temperature over the right arm and right thorax corresponding to dermatomes C5–T12. Pupils were equal and reactive; eyelids were not droopy. Neurological examination showed no sensory deficits or abnormal reflexes.

He had no history of smoking, trauma, or asbestos exposure. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and varicose veins, treated with candesartan and ezetimibe. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000/μL and C-reactive protein of 1.14 mg/dL. Intravenous antibiotics were started on admission, but his symptoms, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings did not improve. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes a patient with a lung mass and symptoms suggestive of a Pancoast tumor, but there is no definitive pathological diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

decisive_spans: transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy
bronchoalveolar lavage revealed ... no microorganisms or malignant cells
reviewer_b.rationale: The record describes a lung mass with Pancoast-like features, but the reference specifies squamous cell carcinoma, a histologic subtype not supported by the record. Biopsy showed no malignancy. The clinical presentation may suggest a neoplastic process, but histologic subtype cannot be identified.

clinical_record:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

decisive_spans: concern for ovarian torsion
reviewer_a.rationale: The record indicates 'concern for ovarian torsion' and describes an adnexal cyst, but there is no specific mention or evidence to support the 'tubo-ovarian complex' component of the reference diagnosis. The imaging did not show a 'whirlpool sign' or 'absent Doppler flow', which are common indicators of torsion, making the specific 'tubo-ovarian complex torsion' unsupported.

decisive_spans: concern for ovarian torsion
left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance
acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers
reviewer_b.rationale: The record explicitly mentions concern for ovarian torsion and describes an adnexal cyst with acute pain and rising inflammatory markers, but it does not provide imaging or surgical evidence that the fallopian tube is involved or that the torsion involves the entire tubo-ovarian complex. Thus, the full specificity of 'tubo-ovarian complex torsion' is not uniquely supported.
unsupported_components: tubo-ovarian complex involvement (fallopian tube not explicitly mentioned)
torsion of the entire complex vs. isolated ovarian torsion

A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a moderately tender mass in the umbilical region. There was non-tender thickening of the right spermatic cord without scrotal or testicular abnormalities; inguinal nodes were barely palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Complete blood counts and blood chemistry were within normal limits, and blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, well-defined, unilocular cyst measuring 20 × 14 × 23 cm located behind the right colon and terminal ileum, without features suggestive of an abscess; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed these findings but did not clarify the origin or etiology of the cyst. Because of diagnostic uncertainty and ongoing symptoms, the abdomen was explored surgically, revealing a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes a retroperitoneal cyst and dilated lymphatics, but there is no mention of filariasis or any parasitic infection. Blood cultures were sterile, and there are no other findings to suggest filariasis as the etiology.

decisive_spans: a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum
a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed
reviewer_b.rationale: The clinical record describes a retroperitoneal cystic lesion with dilated lymphatics, which could support a lymphatic malformation, but there is no mention of filariasis, eosinophilia, or any serologic or microbiologic evidence. The reference diagnosis 'filariasis' is not identifiable from the provided information.

A 27-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of fever and rapidly progressive fullness in the throat, pain on swallowing, dysphagia, and dyspnea. On examination, there was local redness at the root of the tongue but no other mucosal inflammation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with a left shift and elevated C-reactive protein; thyroid-stimulating hormone, triiodothyronine, and thyroxine levels were normal. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a non-homogeneous, mass-like prominence at the base of the tongue compressing the epiglottis and narrowing the pharynx. Neck ultrasound failed to identify the thyroid gland in its normal pretracheal location. Contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrated a 1.7 cm non-homogeneous, contrast-enhancing area at the tongue base with peripheral calcifications; several adjacent 1 cm nodular structures enhanced similarly to thyroid tissue, and no thyroid gland was seen in the usual neck location.

A 61-year-old man with a 20-year history of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating, and obstipation, alternating with intermittent diarrhea, and a 30-lb weight loss presented for evaluation. His history included heavy alcohol use (12–24 beers daily for 20 years) and an uncomplicated cholecystectomy 10 years earlier, after which symptoms began eight days postoperatively. Over the next decade, colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no abnormalities, “including any evidence of celiac disease.” A trial of conservative management failed, and exploratory laparotomy “showed no mechanical cause of the obstructions.” Alcohol use stopped 2 years ago because of worsening symptoms. Fifteen months after the first surgery, a CT scan showed small-bowel dilation (approximately 23 mm in diameter) consistent with obstruction and a concurrent megacolon dilated up to 15 cm. Laboratory studies revealed low levels of fat-soluble vitamins: vitamin A 22 µg/dL (reference, 32.5–78.0), vitamin D 7 ng/mL (20–50), vitamin E 4.3 mg/L (5.5–17), and vitamin K 2.65 ng/mL (0.23–3.2). A gluten-free diet trialed for 3 months produced no improvement.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record describes symptoms consistent with intestinal pseudo-obstruction, including small-bowel dilation and megacolon, but there is no mention or evidence supporting 'Brown bowel syndrome'.

decisive_spans: recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating, and obstipation
small-bowel dilation ... consistent with obstruction and a concurrent megacolon
low levels of fat-soluble vitamins
reviewer_b.rationale: The record supports chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction with malabsorption, but brown bowel syndrome requires histologic confirmation of brown pigmentation of the muscularis propria, which is not provided or implied by the clinical data.

A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record explicitly states that 'cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis' but does not provide definitive evidence to confirm it as the most likely diagnosis. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia (ARVD) is stated as 'highly suspected' with multiple supporting findings.

decisive_spans: cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis
arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed
reviewer_b.rationale: The record explicitly states ARVD was highly suspected and cardiac sarcoidosis remained only a differential diagnosis. No diagnostic test (e.g., CMR, biopsy) was performed to confirm sarcoidosis, and the clinical features are more consistent with ARVD. The reference diagnosis is not uniquely supported by the record.
unsupported_components: cardiac sarcoidosis as most likely diagnosis

A 25-year-old man with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a 2-month history of a gradually enlarging mass over the dorsum of his left hand. Six years earlier, he had been diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma on the basis of mediastinal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms, and he received 13 courses of chemotherapy. Physical examination at this visit revealed a soft-tissue mass over the second metacarpal dorsum, approximately 4 cm in greatest dimension, with mild tenderness and no limitation of movement. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and two specimens were submitted to pathology. The larger specimen consisted of gray, gelatinous tissue measuring 4 × 2.5 × 0.8 cm and 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 cm. Microscopic examination showed a mixture of inflammatory cells, abundant myxoid stroma, epithelioid and spindle-shaped cells, lipoblast-like cells, and occasional Reed–Sternberg–like cells. Given the presence of Reed–Sternberg–like cells in an inflammatory background, the pathologist recommended immunohistochemical staining to distinguish among possible diagnoses.

An 18-year-old man presented with 20 days of pain and swelling around his right scapula, which had been gradually increasing in size, and 2 days of fever. He had been receiving anti-tubercular therapy for presumed pulmonary tuberculosis for 6 months; the diagnosis had been based on cough, chest radiograph findings, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with negative sputum studies. Despite continued therapy, 3 days before presentation he developed swelling and pain of the left ankle with difficulty walking. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 73 mm/h and a positive C-reactive protein level of 96 mg/L. Magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder and left ankle demonstrated findings consistent with osteomyelitis involving the scapula and the distal tibia. An aspiration of the scapular swelling was performed, and specimens were sent for culture, sensitivity testing, and histopathologic examination for possible multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

A 14-year-old boy was referred from a mission hospital for postoperative wound sepsis after right scrotal exploration and orchidectomy for testicular torsion. He had 24 h of scrotal pain and swelling before surgery. On arrival he was tachypneic, tachycardic (124 bpm), febrile (38.7 °C), and diaphoretic, with pallor of mucous membranes. Blood pressure was 109/68 mmHg, neck veins were flat, and heart sounds were normal. The tips of his fingers and toes appeared cyanosed bilaterally with peripheral oxygen saturations fluctuating between 20% and 30% on room air, despite no severe dyspnea. Ecchymoses were present over the extremities, and he bled easily from puncture sites. The right groin wound appeared necrotic and septic. He had no chronic illnesses or medications and denied smoking.  

Initial laboratory studies showed white blood cells 16 × 10^3/µL with neutrophils 10.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, and platelets 26 × 10^3/µL; liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, malaria smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. A diagnosis of severe sepsis complicated by DIC and anemia was made, and he received broad-spectrum antibiotics, blood and platelet transfusions, and surgical debridement.  

Despite improvement in systemic parameters and extubation on day 6, cyanosis of fingers and toes progressed to well-demarcated gangrene below the elbows and knees. A contrast angiogram of the aorta and its branches showed patent thoracic and abdominal aorta and no filling defects in major limb arteries.

reviewer_a.rationale: The clinical record explicitly describes the progression to well-demarcated gangrene of the fingers and toes, which is characteristic of symmetrical peripheral gangrene.

well-demarcated gangrene below the elbows and knees
patent thoracic and abdominal aorta and no filling defects in major limb arteries
reviewer_b.rationale: The record describes a classic presentation of symmetrical peripheral gangrene: sepsis with DIC leading to distal gangrene with patent large vessels. The diagnosis is not explicitly stated but is uniquely supported by the clinical and angiographic findings.

An 86-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of skin lesions on his abdomen and lower back. He reported occasional blurry vision and joint aches but denied weight loss, chills, abdominal pain, bleeding, or healing problems. His medical history was notable only for a 20–pack-year smoking history (quit 50 years ago) and no history of skin cancer. On examination, there were numerous moderately severe, irregular, erythematous papules and nodules on the abdomen and lower back. Laboratory results from 1 month earlier showed leukopenia (white cells 1,900/μL), anemia (3.24 million RBC/μL), mild thrombocytopenia (128,000/μL), and neutropenia (766/μL). C-reactive protein was elevated at 19.5 mg/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 249 U/L. A panel for sexually transmitted infections was negative. A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma.
